title: Social Story Corner
strapline: Little illustrated stories about our own situations — what happens, why, and what I can do — to make the social world make sense.
intent: Children who find social situations baffling get a calm, rehearsable account of what happens and what's expected.
Children prepare for changes and new events — a new room, a trip to the dentist, a new baby at home — before living them.
Children learn the 'hidden rules' of everyday moments (waiting your turn, using an indoor voice) told warmly, not as a telling-off.
Children build strategies for tricky feelings and situations they can recall when the real moment comes.
Children see themselves as the capable hero of the story — someone who can handle this.
implementation: Write short, first-person, positive stories about the child's real situations, using their photos and their world — original to your setting, never a bought pack.
Describe what happens and why, gently, before ever suggesting what to do: understanding first, expectation second.
Keep the tone reassuring and strengths-based — 'sometimes it's noisy at group time, and I can hold my fidget; that's OK' — not a list of don'ts.
Read the relevant story calmly before the situation arises, not in the heat of it, and revisit it often so it's familiar.
Store the stories where a child can fetch their own — a labelled box or a personal folder — and let them choose to reread.
Review and update stories as situations change and always co-create with family so home and setting tell it the same way.
key_questions: What happens in this part of the story?
How does the child in the story feel?
What could they try that might help?
Has this ever happened to you?
Shall we read your story before we go?

impact.text: Children talk about feelings, what caused them, and what helps them feel better.
Children handle a change or new event more calmly because they rehearsed it.
Children resolve minor conflicts increasingly reaching for words and known strategies first.
Children talk about stories, what's happening and what might happen next, mapping them to real life.
Children begin to notice how others feel and act on it.

enhancements: A photo story built the day before a real event — a fire drill, a new key person, moving up a room.
Puppets or small-world figures to act the story out, giving children a safe rehearsal.
A 'my strategies' page at the back of each story listing what helps this particular child.
A shared home-setting version so parents can read the same story at bedtime.
Comic-strip conversations — quick sketched speech bubbles — to unpick a specific incident together afterwards.

playing_exploring: Children explore social situations safely in story form before meeting them for real.
Acting the stories out with puppets turns rehearsal into play.
active_learning: Children choose to reread the story that helps them, showing they value the strategy.
Successfully handling a real moment they rehearsed builds confidence to face the next.
creating_thinking: Children connect the story to their own lives and predict what they might do.
They start to generate their own solutions for tricky moments, drawing on the stories.
